title: ന്യൂനമർദ്ദ പാത്തി: സംസ്ഥാനത്ത് വീണ്ടും മഴ ശക്തമാകുന്നു; ഇന്ന് 9 ജില്ലകളിൽ... - Times Kerala
search_term: (ദുരിതാശ്വാസം OR മുന്നറിയിപ്പ് OR "റെഡ് അലര്‍ട്ട്" OR "ഓറഞ്ച് അലര്‍ട്ട്" OR "യെല്ലോ അലര്‍ട്ട്" OR "ദുരിതാശ്വാസ ക്യാമ്പ്" OR നഷ്ടപരിഹാരം) Kerala
full_text:
തിരുവനന്തപുരം: കന്യാകുമാരി മേഖലയിൽ നിന്ന് തമിഴ്നാടിനും കേരളത്തിനും കുറുകെ തെക്കൻ ഉൾനാടൻ കർണാടക വരെ കിഴക്കൻ കാറ്റുമായി ബന്ധപ്പെട്ട് ന്യൂനമർദ്ദ പാത്തി നിലനിൽക്കുന്നതിനാൽ സംസ്ഥാനത്ത് വീണ്ടും മഴ ശക്തമാകുന്നു. നവംബർ 26, 27 തീയതികളിൽ കേരളത്തിൽ ഒറ്റപ്പെട്ടയിടങ്ങളിൽ ശക്തമായ മഴയ്ക്ക് സാധ്യതയുണ്ടെന്ന് കേന്ദ്ര കാലാവസ്ഥ വകുപ്പ് അറിയിച്ചു.(Kerala Rain Alert, IMD Issues Yellow Alert In Nine Kerala Districts)
മഴയ്ക്കൊപ്പം ഇടിമിന്നലിനും ശക്തമായ കാറ്റിനും സാധ്യതയുള്ളതിനാൽ ജാഗ്രത പാലിക്കണമെന്ന് മുന്നറിയിപ്പുണ്ട്. ഇന്ന് മുതൽ നവംബർ 28 വരെ സംസ്ഥാനത്തെ വിവിധ ഭാഗങ്ങളിൽ ഇടിമിന്നലോടു കൂടിയ മഴയ്ക്കും മണിക്കൂറിൽ 30 മുതൽ 40 കിലോമീറ്റർ വരെ വേഗതയിൽ കാറ്റ് വീശാനും സാധ്യതയുണ്ട്. ശക്തമായ മഴ കണക്കിലെടുത്ത് കേന്ദ്ര കാലാവസ്ഥ വകുപ്പ് വിവിധ ജില്ലകളിൽ യെല്ലോ അലർട്ട് പ്രഖ്യാപിച്ചു.
യെല്ലോ അലർട്ട്
നവംബർ 26 (ഇന്ന്): തിരുവനന്തപുരം, കൊല്ലം, പത്തനംതിട്ട, ആലപ്പുഴ, കോട്ടയം, ഇടുക്കി, എറണാകുളം, മലപ്പുറം, കോഴിക്കോട്.
നവംബർ 27 (നാളെ): കോട്ടയം, ഇടുക്കി, എറണാകുളം, മലപ്പുറം, കോഴിക്കോട്, വയനാട്.
ഒറ്റപ്പെട്ട ശക്തമായ മഴയ്ക്കുള്ള സാധ്യതയാണ് ഈ ജില്ലകളിൽ പ്രവചിച്ചിരിക്കുന്നത്. 24 മണിക്കൂറിൽ 64.5 മില്ലിമീറ്റർ മുതൽ 115.5 മില്ലിമീറ്റർ വരെ മഴ ലഭിക്കുന്ന സാഹചര്യത്തെയാണ് കാലാവസ്ഥ വകുപ്പ് ശക്തമായ മഴയായി കണക്കാക്കുന്നത്. ഇടിമിന്നൽ സാധ്യതയുള്ളതിനാൽ പൊതുജനങ്ങൾ പ്രത്യേക ജാഗ്രത പാലിക്കണമെന്നും അധികൃതർ നിർദേശിച്ചു.
Story Summary
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecast isolated heavy rainfall, thunderstorms, and gusty winds across Kerala on November 26 and 27 due to a trough extending from the Comorin area to South Interior Karnataka. A yellow alert has been issued for nine districts today—including Thiruvananthapuram, Ernakulam, and Kozhikode—and six districts tomorrow, with thunderstorm warnings extending through November 28.

title: Keralam’s green energy push at Pinavoor puts forests, elephants and people at risk - The South First
full_text:
Synopsis: A proposed 7 MW hydropower project at Pinavoor in Keralam’s Ernakulam district has triggered strong opposition from residents and environmental groups over fears that it could obstruct elephant corridors, threaten drinking-water sources, worsen flooding and landslide risks, and affect tribal communities. The controversy comes amid the UDF government’s push to expand renewable energy, with protesters demanding independent environmental and safety assessments before the project proceeds.
At a time when Keralam is looking to make a major push for renewable energy, with Chief Minister VD Satheesan himself stressing the need to expand solar power generation and battery storage, a proposed 7 MW small hydropower project at Pinavoor in Ernakulam has run into stiff opposition over its potential environmental costs.
The contradiction is striking: while the state is under pressure to boost power generation to meet rising demand, the project has raised questions about the price its forests, wildlife and local communities may have to pay for adding to the energy pool.
The chief minister recently assessed that the state currently produces only around 15% of its total electricity requirement and that demand is expected to rise by 2030–31.
What has particularly alarmed conservationists and residents is the possibility that a project meant to harness water for electricity could disrupt wild elephant movement, threaten drinking-water sources, aggravate flood risks and affect the lives of forest-dependent communities.
The proposed Cochin Hydro Power (Pinavoor) Private Limited-developed Pinavoor Small Hydropower Project (SHP) requires the diversion of around 3.1798 hectares of forest land.
The project area falls within the Kuttampuzha Ecologically Sensitive Area (ESA), described by the Coexistence Collective, Keralam — a coalition of environmental organisations, scientists, farmers and NGOs — as the only notified ESA in Ernakulam district.
It also called for independent assessments and greater transparency before undertaking any irreversible construction activity.

Citing a compilation of Forest Department inspection records, project documents, hazard maps, satellite imagery and accounts from local communities, the Collective has raised several questions about the project’s suitability for the location.
Even the Forest Department’s site inspection report, they said, flagged concerns over the proposed 930-metre penstock alignment along the slope of Pambuvettupara, elephant movement, tailrace discharge, flooding, wildlife mitigation and compliance with the Forest Rights Act.
The pipeline is planned at ground level, which could create a physical barrier to elephant movement.
The inspection report noted existing elephant paths in the area. It warned that the pipeline could obstruct their free movement, possibly diverting the animals toward Pinavoorkudy settlement and other inhabited areas.

The project’s possible impact on local water sources is another major concern, particularly in a region that already experiences seasonal scarcity.
Residents alleged that a forest stream linked to the Mamalakkandam Thalippara drinking-water scheme under the Jal Jeevan Mission has been drying up since the project activities began.
The drinking-water scheme, reportedly costing around ₹10 crore, serves approximately 600 families.
However, residents said the streams in the region carry adequate water for only five to six months, while December to May sees severe shortages.
They also pointed out that around 150 tanker loads of water were supplied to two wards during 2025-26, reportedly sourced from a Kerala Water Authority distribution point about 16 km away.
Residents expressed fear that any diversion or modification of the Mamala stream could further compromise water availability. The Coexistence Collective has called for a detailed hydrological assessment covering summer flows, environmental flow requirements, downstream users and the reliability of the drinking-water scheme.

The project’s proximity to the Anandankudy area of the Pinavoorkudy tribal settlement has raised additional concerns.
The Forest Department inspection report called for completion of the certification process related to settling rights under the Forest Rights Act. It also noted that the project proposes to use an existing road passing through the settlement and recommends obtaining the consent of the Forest Rights Committee.
Residents and conservationists sought clarity on whether the statutory safeguards, community consultation requirements and rights of affected tribal families have been fully addressed.
The manner in which the project received local approval has also become contentious.
Residents alleged that the Kuttampuzha Grama Panchayat issued a no-objection certificate (NOC) in 2023 without adequately informing the affected communities. They said they learned about the proposal only on 29 July 2025, when Forest Department officials visited the site.
Opposition to the project gained momentum in July 2026, when residents staged protest marches and a dharna at the Kuttampuzha Panchayat office. Hundreds of people from two wards participated, demanding that the project be abandoned and citing threats to their livelihoods, water sources, and the surrounding environment.
Satheesh, a member of the Mamalakkandam Samrakshana Samithi and a resident, said the project could aggravate the difficulties already faced by people living in the region.
“We are not opposed to development or electricity generation. But a project of this scale in a forest-fringe area like Pinavoor cannot be viewed merely as a power-generation initiative. Our drinking-water sources are already unreliable, elephants regularly move through this landscape, and several areas are vulnerable to flooding and landslides. Diverting streams, laying pipelines along elephant routes and carrying out construction in such a fragile terrain could put both people and wildlife at risk. It is the local community that will have to live with the consequences long after the project is completed,” the resident said.
Satheesh further added, “Development should not come at the cost of the safety and livelihood of the people here.”

The proposed diversion of forest land has also brought the compensatory afforestation plan under scrutiny.
The collective has questioned the ecological suitability and current status of the land identified for compensatory planting, as well as whether the proposed plantation would genuinely compensate for the loss of an existing forest ecosystem.
It has sought disclosure of the afforestation plan, including the site’s status, suitability, additionality and long-term survival prospects.
The proposed disposal of excavated material, or muck, generated during tunnelling is another issue requiring examination. Improper disposal in a steep forest landscape could affect natural drainage, slopes and nearby watercourses.
Advocate Santhosh TS, legal adviser to the Animal and Nature Ethics Community, an NGO, has also raised concerns about the project’s environmental and legal implications.
“The issue is not simply whether a 7 MW project can generate electricity. It is whether the project can be implemented without compromising the ecological integrity of the region, wildlife movement and the rights and safety of the people living there,” he said.
Santhosh said the various concerns should be examined together, rather than through separate clearances that may fail to account for the project’s cumulative impact.
“Elephant movement, water availability, flood vulnerability, tribal rights and geological stability are interconnected issues in a landscape like Pinavoor. A clearance process must take into account the ground realities and the people who will bear the consequences if something goes wrong,” he said.

The Coexistence Collective has called for the disclosure of all project and forest-diversion documents and independent studies on hydrology, flood risks, geological stability, tunnel safety and wildlife movement.
It has also demanded verification of the ESA notification and KSDMA hazard classifications, a review of Forest Rights Act compliance, an assessment of muck disposal arrangements and an independent examination of the compensatory-afforestation proposal.
The group demanded transparent public consultations and a detailed assessment of the cumulative environmental impact before construction proceeds. It also called for suspending irreversible work until the outstanding statutory, ecological, and public-safety concerns are satisfactorily addressed.
(Edited by Majnu Babu).
